slides.title: The lab needs a forecast for its weekly review
slides.body:
Fictional lab · the principal investigator

“Does the model predict anything better than assuming the Sun stays as it is?”

Your assignment

Use observations from February 1–14, 2014 to test that question. Bring a forecast, its errors, and the code a colleague needs to repeat it.

The lab is fictional. The satellite observations are real.
slides.notes: The principal investigator, or PI, runs the weekly research meeting. You are the researcher preparing a comparison for that meeting. The question is deliberately concrete: does a trained model predict the next observation better than simply copying the current one? We have two weeks of archived data, so we can hide later observations, make predictions, and then compare them with what was actually recorded. We are practicing an experiment design; these short runs cannot establish reliable solar forecasting. Session block: Connect and trace an operation (minutes 0–25).
slides.concept: The lab needs a forecast for its weekly review

slides.title: What the satellites recorded
slides.body:
Actual archive observations. NOAA GOES-15 and NASA/SDO AIA; false-color image.

GOES-15: two whole-Sun X-ray readings each minute, measured in watts per square metre.

AIA 171 Å: an extreme-ultraviolet view of the Sun’s outer atmosphere, reduced to 64 × 64 pixels.
slides.notes: GOES gives us two numerical measurements each minute: XRS-A and XRS-B measure X-ray power per square metre in different wavelength bands. The plot shows XRS-B, transformed with log10 because its values span a wide range. AIA is a different instrument on NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. Its 171-angstrom images show extreme-ultraviolet emission from the Sun’s outer atmosphere. The colors represent intensity, not visible light or a direct temperature measurement. Our teaching arrays reduce the images to sixty-four by sixty-four pixels. SunPy retrieves and reads the observations and metadata; our preprocessing code builds the training arrays. These are separate forecasting tasks, not two inputs to one model. Sources: https://www.spaceweather.gov/products/goes-x-ray-flux and https://sdo.gsfc.nasa.gov/data/channels.php. Session block: Connect and trace an operation (minutes 0–25).

slides.title: What one forecast example contains
slides.body: Persistence predicts no change. A trained model must beat it on the same future observations.
slides.notes: Both examples shown here exist in the prepared training data. Set the clock to 01:00 UTC on February 1. For GOES, the model can read sixty one-minute samples in each channel, from 00:01 through 01:00, and must predict XRS-B at 01:30. Persistence uses only the current XRS-B reading as that forecast. For AIA, the model sees images from 00:00 and 01:00 and predicts the image at 02:00; persistence copies the 01:00 image. The future observations are targets for scoring, never inputs to the prediction. We compare absolute error in log-flux units for GOES and mean absolute error in normalized image intensity inside the solar disk for AIA. The scores stay separate. If little changes over the horizon, copying the latest observation can be hard to beat. We will measure that rather than assume the trained model wins. Session block: Connect and trace an operation (minutes 0–25).

slides.title: Use different dates to fit, choose, and evaluate
slides.body: February 2014, UTC. Each example’s inputs and target stay inside one date partition.
slides.notes: These dates serve three different research decisions. February 1–10 trains the model weights and supplies the normalization statistics. slides.title: Separate prediction, gradients and the optimizer step
slides.body:
```python {1-2|3|4|5|all} prediction = model(batch_x) loss = training_loss(prediction, batch_y, mask) optimizer.zero_grad() loss.backward() optimizer.step() ```
A forward pass returns predictions. Only the optimizer step changes model parameters.
slides.notes: zero_grad clears accumulated gradients; PyTorch adds new gradients unless we clear them. The forward pass creates predictions and records the operations needed for differentiation. backward computes derivatives of the loss with respect to trainable parameters. step applies the optimizer update. The workshop loops over a fixed number of optimizer steps, not a promised number of full dataset epochs. Training sample order and initialization depend on the seed. slides.title: Let the model learn a correction to persistence
slides.body:
```python {2|3|4|all} def forward(self, x): correction = self.net(x) standardized = x[:, 1, -1:] + correction return standardized * self.scale + self.center # Zero-initialize the correction head before training. # Fit scaling on training dates; score in log-flux units. ```
The repair also uses absolute loss and 1,200 updates. These choices are tested together.
slides.notes: The latest XRS-B input is standardized. Add a learned correction, then convert it back with the same training-fitted center and scale. A zero-initialized final layer begins exactly at persistence. The fit function divides the prediction and target error by the same scale. We changed several parts of the recipe together, so the measured result cannot tell us which individual change caused the gain. Ask participants to point to the addition and unit conversion in their editable code. Advance the code highlights one step at a time; use Back to revisit the previous statement.

slides.title: Average the error inside the disk mask
slides.body:
```python def my_image_mae(prediction, target, disk_mask): errors = np.abs(prediction - target) * disk_mask per_image = errors.sum(axis=(1, 2, 3)) per_image /= disk_mask.sum(axis=(1, 2, 3)) return float(per_image.mean()) ```

Test zero error, constant +1 error, and an error only outside the mask.
slides.notes: The mask selects the solar disk. Compute the sum and count per image, then average across images. Check identical arrays, a constant one-unit difference, and a difference only outside the mask.
slides.concept: Average the error inside the disk mask

slides.notes: Channel zero is the earlier image and channel one is the current image. Add the correction to channel one. With a zero correction, this function returns the current image exactly.
